lesson.title: Straight-Line Thinking: First-Order Reactions
lesson.summary: In a first-order reaction, rate is directly proportional to the concentration of a single reactant raised to the first power, so doubling that concentration doubles the rate and halving it halves the rate.
lesson.body:
A first-order reaction is one where the reaction order with respect to a given reactant is 1, giving a rate law of the form rate = k[A]. Unlike the zero order case, here the rate genuinely tracks the concentration: if you double [A], the rate doubles; if you cut [A] in half, the rate is cut in half. The relationship is directly proportional, which is the simplest and, in many ways, the most intuitive kind of concentration dependence.

Physically, first order behavior is common for reactions where a single molecule of A has to do something on its own before the reaction can proceed, break apart, isomerize, or otherwise transform, without needing to first collide with another reactant molecule. Since the number of A molecules available to undergo that spontaneous change scales directly with [A], the overall rate scales the same way. This is analogous to radioactive decay, where the number of decay events per second is directly proportional to how many undecayed atoms remain.

Consider a first order reaction with rate constant k = 0.030 s^-1. At [A] = 0.50 M, the rate is rate = k[A] = 0.030 s^-1 x 0.50 M = 0.015 M/s. Now suppose [A] falls to 0.25 M, exactly half its earlier value. The rate becomes rate = k[A] = 0.030 s^-1 x 0.25 M = 0.0075 M/s, which is exactly half of 0.015 M/s. The rate tracked the concentration change precisely: halve the concentration, halve the rate.

Notice also, as the rate constant chapter established, that k for a first order reaction carries units of inverse time (here, s^-1) with no concentration unit attached at all. That is a direct consequence of the concentration term [A] in the rate law already carrying one full power of M, which cancels the M in the M/s rate to leave only s^-1 behind. One further hallmark of first order kinetics, that the time it takes for the concentration to fall by half stays constant no matter what concentration you start from, is a striking result you will derive properly once you reach the integrated rate law for first order reactions later in your studies. For now, the essential picture is proportionality: first order means rate and concentration rise and fall together, in lockstep.
